ReVEAL: Eliciting Role-Aware Latent Visual Evidence from MLLMs for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation

Zhongyuan Bao Affiliation: Fudan University    Cunjie He Affiliation: Fudan University    Lejun Zhang Affiliation: New York University    Zenglin Xu Affiliation: Fudan University    Yanwei Fu Affiliation: Fudan University
Abstract

Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) requires segmenting the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. Existing MLLM-based methods typically require costly cross-model alignment, tying MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model. We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to directly guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) into video reasoning to associate necessary visual regions or entities with target, background, or distractor roles, while a Dynamic Attention Layer Router adaptively aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. We train the MLLM to perform VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision to apply role-specific constraints to VET attention and optimize layer routing for reliable latent grounding. At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through this thinking-with-video process and fuses the resulting role-specific evidence to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks. Experiments on five benchmarks show that ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.

1 Introduction

Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (ReVOS) aims to segment target objects throughout a video according to free-form and often implicit language expressions. Unlike conventional referring video object segmentation (RVOS), the target may not be identifiable from a single frame or an explicit category name. Instead, it relies on the model’s ability to perceive and understand the video content in relation to the query, such as identifying “the object used to keep the drink cold”. This makes Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) (Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023) a natural backbone for ReVOS. However, the challenge is not only to understand the expression, but also to connect such understanding to the visual evidence that supports a consistent object mask across time.

Since MLLMs do not directly produce pixel masks, existing MLLM-based ReVOS methods typically rely on cross-modal alignment with an external segmenter, making MLLM training dependent on the downstream segmentation model. Existing approaches often introduce a dedicated segmentation token, such as <SEG>, and align its hidden representation with the prompt space of an external segmenter (Kirillov et al., 2023; Ravi et al., 2025). Although straightforward for mask generation, such design incurs additional training costs and ties the framework to a specific MLLM–segmenter pair, complicating adaptation to alternative backbones and downstream settings.

Recent reasoning MLLMs adopt a thinking-with-images paradigm that incorporates visual primitives into intermediate chain-of-thoughts (CoT) steps, using boxes and points (OpenAI, 2025; Liu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b) or special tokens (Qin et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). This paradigm extends to thinking-with-video, where spatio-temporal cues serve as intermediate references for reasoning across frames (Zhang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2025). Interactive video segmentation models such as SAM2 (Ravi et al., 2025) likewise accept spatial primitives as prompts for object identification and mask propagation, providing a natural interface through which visual evidence produced during MLLM reasoning can directly guide segmentation (Kao et al., 2025).

Yet these primitives are typically limited to selected keyframes (Gong et al., 2025a; Zhong et al., 2026), providing only sparse grounding evidence across the video. Causal self-attention, on the other hand, offers a denser alternative (Vaswani et al., 2017): text tokens attend to visual tokens across preceding frames, yielding video-wide attention maps with spatial grounding cues (Li et al., 2025), although these cues may not reliably localize the corresponding regions (Jang et al., 2026). DecAF (Han et al., 2025) relies on a tailored multi-rollout procedure to obtain object and background attention maps for segmentation, incurring substantial inference cost without leveraging video reasoning itself. This motivates us to explore whether an MLLM can produce the grounding evidence needed for segmentation as part of its own video reasoning within a single response.

To this end, we present ReVEAL, a thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) to mark necessary visual regions or entities as target (<OBJ>), background (<BG>), or distractors (<NEG>) during reasoning. A Dynamic Attention Layer Router (DALR) learns to adaptively aggregate their attention over preceding visual tokens across Transformer layers into role-specific evidence maps. To enable the MLLM to elicit faithful role-aware latent visual evidence through video reasoning, we perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, using a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss (CAGL) as auxiliary supervision to optimize layer routing and apply role-specific constraints to VET attention over video tokens for reliable latent grounding.

At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through VET-augmented video reasoning. DALR then aggregates VET-to-video attention from the CoT across Transformer layers into role-specific evidence. These attention maps are then contrastively fused, and point prompts are sampled from high-confidence regions to guide a frozen external SAM2 in predicting the target masks, forming an alignment-free interface between MLLM reasoning and video object segmentation.

In a nutshell, our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence during MLLM reasoning to guide segmentation without cross-model alignment.

  • •

    We equip the MLLM with this capability by combining reasoning supervision on ReVEAL-47K with CAGL for attention grounding over layers adaptively selected and weighted by DALR.

  • •

    We demonstrate that internal signals from MLLM reasoning can provide effective grounding cues for video object segmentation through experiments on five RVOS and ReVOS benchmarks.

2 Related Work

2.1 Multimodal Large Language Models

Building on the success of LLMs in natural language processing, image MLLMs extend language models to visual inputs by bridging visual features into the language model through cross-attention resamplers (Alayrac et al., 2022), querying transformers (Li et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023), or projection-based visual instruction tuning (Liu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024). Subsequent systems further scale visual backbones and training data to improve general vision–language capabilities (Chen et al., 2024b; Bai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Video MLLMs extend this paradigm to video by incorporating sampled-frame representations and temporal modeling (Zhang et al., 2023; Maaz et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026). Beyond general video understanding, recent work increasingly adopts video MLLMs as general-purpose backbones for downstream tasks that require fine-grained perception and reasoning, including dense video captioning (Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2024), temporal grounding (Ren et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2024a), subject-specific video question answering (Yuan et al., 2025c; Lian et al., 2025), and embodied spatial reasoning (Yang et al., 2025). We extend this line of research to ReVOS by leveraging MLLMs’ spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities to identify target objects specified by complex queries.

2.2 Referring and Reasoning Video Object Segmentation

Referring Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) segments an object in a video based on a natural language expression. Early methods focus on explicit expressions through cross-modal fusion or query propagation (Seo et al., 2020; Botach et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022). Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (ReVOS) extends this task to implicit queries that identify targets through their functions, behaviors, or relations to other objects, requiring more complex reasoning (Yan et al., 2024). Most MLLM-based methods interpret implicit queries and learn cross-modal alignment by mapping the hidden state of a special <SEG> token to a downstream segmenter’s prompt space for mask prediction (Lai et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025b). Recent work promotes this alignment indirectly through reinforcement learning, using SAM2-based segmentation rewards to optimize key-frame selection and MLLM-generated bounding boxes (Gong et al., 2025a; Zhong et al., 2026). Both strategies tie MLLM training to a downstream segmenter, leaving the potential of native MLLM reasoning as an independent source of visual grounding evidence underexplored (Kao et al., 2025). In contrast, we train the MLLM under a thinking-with-video paradigm to elicit latent grounding evidence from video reasoning and use this evidence to guide an external segmenter at inference.

2.3 Visual Evidence in MLLM Reasoning

OpenAI-o3 (OpenAI, 2025) introduces a thinking-with-images paradigm that incorporates references to visual regions into intermediate reasoning steps. Recent methods explicitly refer to these regions using boxes and points (Liu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b) or special tokens representing masks and image patches (Qin et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025b). This idea also extends to thinking-with-video, where spatio-temporal cues serve as references for video reasoning (Meng et al., 2025). However, generating such references throughout a video becomes cumbersome for dense video prediction. Instead, attention from output tokens to the preceding multimodal context provides a potential source of latent grounding evidence by highlighting visual regions associated with token semantics (Kang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026; Vaswani et al., 2017). Despite this potential, raw attention is often noisy and susceptible to attention sinks (Huang et al., 2024b; Darcet et al., 2024), limiting its reliability as visual evidence. InterRVOS (Jin et al., 2026) constrains attention to relevant object regions to enrich semantic representations during cross-model alignment, whereas DecAF (Han et al., 2025) aggregates attention maps across multiple queries for visual grounding. In contrast, ReVEAL derives role-aware latent visual evidence directly from video reasoning and fuses those cues for more accurate target localization.

3 Method

Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) aims to segment the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. We propose ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework that uses role-aware latent evidence from MLLM reasoning to guide segmentation. During training, the MLLM learns to use VETs as role-specific semantic anchors for necessary visual regions or entities, with spatio-temporal grounding constraints applied directly to its own attention rather than through alignment with a downstream segmenter. At inference, ReVEAL derives role-specific latent visual evidence through VET-augmented video reasoning and fuses this evidence as grounding signals to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks.

Taxonomy of VETs.

ReVEAL augments the MLLM vocabulary 𝒱orig\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{orig}} with three role-specific VETs: <OBJ> specifies the referred target, <NEG> identifies the foreground distractor to exclude, and <BG> indicates the background region to suppress:

𝒱=𝒱orig∪𝒱VET𝒱VET={<OBJ>,<BG>,<NEG>}\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{orig}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{VET}}\qquad\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{VET}}=\{\texttt{<OBJ>},\texttt{<BG>},\texttt{<NEG>}\} (1)

Obtaining VET Attention Maps.

We treat each VET’s attention to the preceding visual tokens as a role-specific latent grounding cue. The corresponding attention map is obtained by aggregating these cues across Transformer layers, with later layers selected as candidates because they generally encode stronger semantic signals (Han et al., 2025). Let ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} denote the set of LcL_{c} candidate layers and A∈[0,1]Lc×N×NA\in[0,1]^{L_{c}\times N\times N} collect their post-softmax attention weights averaged across heads, where NN is the whole sequence length. For the jj-th VET occurrence with role rr, we extract its attention weights over the preceding video tokens and reshape them into layer-wise attention maps ar,j∈[0,1]Lc×T×Hv×Wva^{r,j}\in[0,1]^{L_{c}\times T\times H_{v}\times W_{v}}, where TT is the number of frames and HvH_{v} and WvW_{v} denote the height and width of each frame’s visual token grid.

However, the layers most relevant to target grounding may vary across different cases (Kang et al., 2025). Inspired by mixture-of-experts routing (Liu et al., 2024), we introduce a Dynamic Attention Layer Router (DALR) to dynamically select and weight candidate layers based on the <OBJ> attention maps. Given the <OBJ> attention maps for each video-query pair, DALR scores the candidate layers, selects the top-kk layers as 𝒮⊂ℒc\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{L}_{c}, and normalizes their scores into routing weights wlw_{l}. These weights determine the contribution of each selected layer when aggregating VET attention during both training and inference. More details are provided in Appendix B.

3.1 Learning Video Reasoning with VETs

Supervising Thinking-with-video Reasoning.

Through SFT, the MLLM learns to identify query-relevant visual entities or regions during video reasoning and place the corresponding role-specific VETs after their names or descriptions, conditioning each VET occurrence on an entity-specific context. Given a video VV, a query qq, and a VET-augmented response 𝐮=(u1,…,uM)\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{M}), we optimize the model using the standard next token prediction objective:

ℒSFT=−∑i=1Mlogp(ui∣u<i,V,q).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{M}\log p\!\left(u_{i}\mid u_{<i},V,q\right). (2)

Let nr​(u)n_{r}(u) denote the number of occurrences of role rr in response uu. Each response contains n<OBJ>​(u)=1n_{\texttt{<OBJ>}}(u)=1 and n<BG>​(u)∈{0,1}n_{\texttt{<BG>}}(u)\in\{0,1\}, while n<NEG>​(u)n_{\texttt{<NEG>}}(u) varies with the number of distinct distractors described in the reasoning trace.

Aligning Attention Maps with Visual Regions.

Although SFT teaches the model to perform VET-augmented video reasoning to identify relevant visual entities and their semantic roles, it does not ensure that VET attention provides reliable latent grounding evidence. Inspired by AML (Jin et al., 2026), we introduce the Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss (CAGL) to supervise the spatio-temporal distribution of VET attention using complementary positive and repulsive terms.

ℒCAGL=∑l∈𝒮wl​(ℒCAGL−Pl+λrep​ℒCAGL−Rl).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL}}=\sum_{l\in\mathcal{S}}w_{l}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL-P}}^{l}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL-R}}^{l}\right). (3)

Here, wlw_{l} is the routing weight assigned by DALR to layer ll, and λrep\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}} balances the repulsive term.

For each occurrence jj of a role r∈𝒫={<OBJ>,<BG>}r\in\mathcal{P}=\{\texttt{<OBJ>},\texttt{<BG>}\}, the positive term applies BCE to align its attention distribution with the corresponding ground-truth (GT) region mr∈[0,1]T×Hv×Wvm^{r}\in[0,1]^{T\times H_{v}\times W_{v}}:

ℒCAGL−Pl=∑r∈𝒫∑j=1nr​(u)BCE⁡(alr,j,mr),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL-P}}^{l}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{r}(u)}\operatorname{BCE}\!\left(a_{l}^{r,j},m^{r}\right), (4)

During reasoning, the attention maps of the suppressive roles r∈ℛ={<BG>,<NEG>}r\in\mathcal{R}=\{\texttt{<BG>},\texttt{<NEG>}\} provide suppressive evidence, but leakage into unintended regions may cause erroneous suppression. We therefore apply a repulsive term that penalizes the normalized attention mass within a role-specific forbidden region frf^{r}. Specifically, we define f<BG>=m<OBJ>f^{\texttt{<BG>}}=m^{\texttt{<OBJ>}} and f<NEG>=m<OBJ>∪m<BG>f^{\texttt{<NEG>}}=m^{\texttt{<OBJ>}}\cup m^{\texttt{<BG>}}:

a^lr,j=alr,j∥alr,j∥1+ϵ,ℒCAGL−Rl=∑r∈ℛ∑j=1nr​(u)−log(1−⟨a^lr,j,fr⟩+ϵ).\hat{a}_{l}^{r,j}=\frac{a_{l}^{r,j}}{\lVert a_{l}^{r,j}\rVert_{1}+\epsilon},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL-R}}^{l}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{r}(u)}-\log\left(1-\left\langle\hat{a}_{l}^{r,j},f^{r}\right\rangle+\epsilon\right). (5)

Here, ∥alr,j∥1\lVert a_{l}^{r,j}\rVert_{1} sums the attention over all spatio-temporal locations, and the inner product ⟨a^lr,j,fr⟩\langle\hat{a}_{l}^{r,j},f^{r}\rangle measures the normalized attention mass within the forbidden region.

Final Training Objective.

The final objective combines SFT with CAGL:

ℒ=ℒSFT+λCAGL​ℒCAGL\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CAGL}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAGL}} (6)

Here, λCAGL\lambda_{\mathrm{CAGL}} controls the strength of CAGL.

Training Data Construction.

To provide supervision for ReVEAL, we construct ReVEAL-47K, a training dataset comprising VET-augmented CoT traces and region-level mask annotations, from multiple training sources (Lai et al., 2024; Khoreva et al., 2018; Seo et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2024). For each sample, we use GAR (Wang et al., 2025c) with the GT mask on a representative frame to obtain a target caption. Conditioned on this caption, the query, and the video frames, Gemini 2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025) generates a CoT response and inserts VETs at the corresponding positions. Qwen3VL (Bai et al., 2025) is used to verify and filter out unreliable samples. The mask annotations include the retained GT mask and a background mask, obtained by taking the complement of the union of the foreground regions predicted by BiRefNet (Zheng et al., 2024a) and the target region. More details are provided in Appendix A.

3.2 From VET Attention Maps to Segmentation Masks

At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through VET-augmented video reasoning. DALR adaptively selects and weights Transformer layers to aggregate VET attention into role-specific latent evidence maps, which are then fused to guide mask prediction with a frozen, external SAM2.

Specifically, the <OBJ> attention is aggregated across the selected layers to form target evidence, whereas attention associated with all <BG> and <NEG> tokens is aggregated as suppressive evidence:

aobj\displaystyle a^{\mathrm{obj}} =∑l∈𝒮wl​al<OBJ>,1,asup\displaystyle=\sum_{l\in\mathcal{S}}w_{l}a_{l}^{\texttt{<OBJ>},1},\ a^{\mathrm{sup}} =∑r∈ℛαr​∑j=1nr​(u)∑l∈𝒮wl​alr,j,\displaystyle=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\alpha_{r}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{r}(u)}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{S}}w_{l}a_{l}^{r,j}, (7)

where αr\alpha_{r} controls the contribution of each suppressive role.

Contrastive Attention Fusion.

We fuse the target and suppressive evidence frame by frame. For frame tt, the corresponding slices atobj,atsup∈ℝHv×Wva_{t}^{\mathrm{obj}},a_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{v}\times W_{v}} are combined by subtracting the suppressive evidence from the target evidence:

P~t=max⁡(atobj−atsup, 0)Pt=P~t−min⁡(P~t)max⁡(P~t)−min⁡(P~t)+ϵ\tilde{P}_{t}=\max\!\left(a_{t}^{\texttt{obj}}-a_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}},\,0\right)\qquad P_{t}=\frac{\tilde{P}_{t}-\min(\tilde{P}_{t})}{\max(\tilde{P}_{t})-\min(\tilde{P}_{t})+\epsilon} (8)

Here, the minimum and maximum are taken over spatial locations, and ϵ\epsilon ensures numerical stability. We then sample points from the fused attention map PtP_{t} as visual prompts for the frozen SAM2.

SAM2 Prompting and Mask Generation.

We apply a threshold τpq\tau_{\mathrm{pq}} to the fused attention map and sample points from the retained regions according to their attention strengths as prompts for SAM2 to generate candidate mask tracklets. Following the SAM2 prompting pipeline of DecAF (Han et al., 2025), we remove redundant candidates using non-maximum suppression with an IoU threshold τnms\tau_{\mathrm{nms}}, ranking them by point-attention and SAM2 confidence scores. We then filter the remaining tracklets by their temporal consistency with the retained attention regions using τtrk\tau_{\mathrm{trk}} and propagate them across all frames to produce the final segmentation masks.

4 Experiments

Datasets and metrics.

We evaluate ReVEAL on five RVOS and ReVOS benchmarks: Ref-DAVIS (Khoreva et al., 2018), Ref-YouTube-VOS (Seo et al., 2020), MeViS (Ding et al., 2023), ReVOS (Yan et al., 2024), and ReasonVOS (Bai et al., 2024). Following standard practice, we report mask quality using region similarity 𝒥\mathcal{J}, boundary accuracy ℱ\mathcal{F}, and their average 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}.

Implementation Details.

ReVEAL uniformly samples six frames from each video as input. We finetune the MLLM using LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024b), with the CAGL weight λCAGL\lambda_{\mathrm{CAGL}} set to 0.2 and the λrep\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}} in CAGL set to 0.1. The router top-kk is set to 6. For inference and evaluation, we use SAM2-Hiera-Large (Ravi et al., 2025) as the frozen segmentation model. We set α<BG>=0.5\alpha_{\mathrm{<BG>}}=0.5 for Qwen2.5-VL and α<BG>=0.1\alpha_{\mathrm{<BG>}}=0.1 for Qwen3VL, while using α<NEG>=1.0\alpha_{\mathrm{<NEG>}}=1.0 for both. All other settings follow the baseline (Han et al., 2025), using a threshold of τpq=0.8\tau_{\mathrm{pq}}=0.8, a NMS IoU threshold of τnms=0.7\tau_{\mathrm{nms}}=0.7, and a tracklet-consistency threshold of τtrk=0.8\tau_{\mathrm{trk}}=0.8. Our experiments are conducted on NVIDIA H800 GPUs. More details are provided in Appendix B.

4.1 Main Results

Masks with Attn.

Table 2 compares ReVEAL with attention-derived grounding methods under the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone and six frame input setting. ReVEAL achieves the best performance across all benchmarks, outperforming DecAF by 5.7%, 3.0%, and 4.6% 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} on Ref-DAVIS, ReasonVOS, and ReVOS. These results indicate that ReVEAL produces attention maps with more complete spatio-temporal coverage of the target regions, providing stronger grounding evidence. Despite these gains, ℱ\mathcal{F} remains relatively low because the coarse attention maps lack precise object boundaries and therefore still require a dedicated segmenter for accurate mask prediction.

Masks with SAM2.

As shown in Table 2, among alignment-free methods, ReVEAL achieves the best performance across all benchmarks. With the same backbone, it outperforms DecAF by 4.8% and 9.3% 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} on ReVOS and Ref-YouTube-VOS, respectively, and consistently outperforms CoT-RVS despite using a smaller backbone. These results suggest that the high-attention regions identified by ReVEAL provide reliable visual prompts for mask generation. While alignment-based methods benefit from cross-model optimization between the MLLM and the segmentation module, ReVEAL approaches the performance of RGA-3 under the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone without costly cross-model adapter training. With Qwen3-VL-8B, ReVEAL achieves the highest scores on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS, surpassing the strongest alignment-based results by 4.3% and 6.2% 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}, respectively, while substantially narrowing the gap on ReVOS, MeViS, and Ref-YouTube-VOS. Additional results are provided in the Appendix C.1

4.2 Ablation Study

In this section, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies. By default, results are reported with ReVEAL-Qwen3VL-8B. Additional results are provided in the Appendix C.2.

Thinking-with-video Paradigm for ReVOS.

Table 7 evaluates the effect of the thinking-with-video paradigm. Without CoT, the model learns to emit VETs within a simple response (e.g., Sure, it is <BG>, <NEG> and <OBJ>.) With CoT, attention-derived mask 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} improves by 1.1% and 1.7% on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS, respectively, while the corresponding SAM2 masks improve by 3.1% and 12.2%. These results show that VET-augmented video reasoning improves grounding beyond simple outputs, providing more effective guidance for downstream segmentation.

Training Components.

Table 7 shows that SFT alone is insufficient for reliable VET grounding. CAGL-P improves target coverage in latent evidence, while CAGL-R makes attention scores in the fused maps more reliable for point selection. DALR further improves evidence aggregation over fixed-layer selection schemes. Together, these components help ReVEAL elicit faithful role-aware visual evidence during video reasoning to guide segmentation.

VET Fusion at Inference.

Table 7 compares different VET attention combinations from the same CoT at inference. Adding <BG> improves attention-mask scores by 3.9% and 4.6% on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS, while adding <NEG> instead yields better SAM2 segmentation despite lower attention-mask scores. This suggests that background suppression refines the overall target coverage, whereas distractor suppression makes attention peaks more discriminative. Combining all three VET types yields the best overall performance, supporting the effectiveness of our role design.

MLLM Backbone Scalability.

As shown in Table 7, ReVEAL consistently outperforms the baseline across diverse MLLM backbones, demonstrating its generalizability. We further observe that the performance generally improves with backbone size. For example, scaling Qwen3VL from 4B to 8B improves 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} by 3.6% on Ref-DAVIS and ReVOS and 5.6% on ReasonVOS, suggesting that larger MLLMs provide more reliable visual evidence for downstream segmentation.

Segmentation Backbone Scalability.

ReVEAL uses latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to guide segmentation without requiring alignment to a specific segmenter. As shown in Table 7, the latent grounding evidence generalizes across smaller SAM2 variants and SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) on all three benchmarks, with minor performance variations due to the segmenter’s own capability.

Qualitative Analysis.

We provide qualitative analysis of ReVEAL from two perspectives. First, Fig. 4 shows that ReVEAL reduces noise in the fused attention maps compared with DecAF, resulting in more precise focus on the target object and more accurate grounding for challenging queries requiring implicit reasoning. Second, Fig. 5 shows that different VETs generally attend to regions consistent with their intended roles. Additional cases are provided in Appendix D.

5 Conclusion

We presented ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for alignment-free ReVOS. ReVEAL enables the MLLM to identify targets through video reasoning and derive grounding cues from role-aware VET attention, without requiring cross-model alignment with the segmenter during training. At inference, ReVEAL derives role-specific evidence from VET-augmented video reasoning to guide a frozen SAM2 for target mask prediction. Experiments across five RVOS and ReVOS benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of ReVEAL. Overall, our work highlights the potential of internal signals from MLLM reasoning to bridge high-level video understanding and dense visual prediction.

AI Use Statement

We use generative AI tools in constructing the ReVEAL-47K training dataset, including video CoT annotation and formatting collected samples into VET-augmented CoT traces, as described in Section 3.1 and the Appendix. GPT is used to polish the manuscript, including language refinement and grammar checking of our original draft. We do not use AI tools for other research tasks requiring disclosure. We review all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the final paper.

Appendix A ReVEAL-47K Training Dataset

A.1 Dataset Overview

To equip the model with dynamic role-aware VET reasoning and reliable latent visual grounding, we construct ReVEAL-47K training dataset, comprising 47K VET-augmented ReVOS CoT traces paired with target and background masks for attention grounding.

ReVEAL-47K is constructed from the training splits of five public RVOS and ReVOS datasets, including MeViS (Ding et al., 2023), ReVOS (Yan et al., 2024), GroundMoRe (Deng et al., 2025), Ref-DAVIS (Khoreva et al., 2018), and Ref-YouTube-VOS (Seo et al., 2020), together with the image reasoning segmentation dataset ReasonSeg (Lai et al., 2024), as shown in Fig. 6. We use six frames as the model input for all samples. For ReasonSeg, each sample is included twice, with its single image repeated across six frames and treated as a static video. The resulting dataset contains 47K VET-augmented CoT annotations. Each trace contains exactly one <OBJ> token for target evidence, even when the query refers to multiple target objects, as its attention map can cover multiple target regions, while suppressive VETs are introduced only when needed. Specifically, <BG> appears at most once to provide background evidence, whereas multiple <NEG> tokens can be used to distinguish different distractors. On average, each trace contains 1.00 <OBJ>, 0.42 <BG>, and 0.86 <NEG> tokens.

Appendix B More Details of ReVEAL

B.1 Dynamic Attention Layer Router

Since target identification is central to ReVOS, DALR uses <OBJ> attention as the routing cue to select layers that provide informative target evidence. As these layers vary across inputs, DALR adaptively selects and weights candidate layers for each sample. The same layer selection and routing weights are applied to all VET roles, ensuring efficient aggregation of role-specific attention maps. As detailed in Algorithm 1, DALR employs noisy top-kk routing during training to encourage exploration and deterministic routing at inference. We use Lc=14L_{c}=14 candidate layers for Qwen2.5VL-7B and Lc=18L_{c}=18 for Qwen3VL-8B, with a feature dimension of 256256 and k=6k=6 by default.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Analysis

By default, results are reported with ReVEAL-Qwen3VL-8B and the 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} metric.

C.1 Additional Quantitative Results

Inference Efficiency.

We compare the efficiency of MLLM-side attention production of ReVEAL with the baseline DecAF (Han et al., 2025) on Ref-DAVIS using the same Qwen2.5VL-7B. As shown in Table 10, ReVEAL requires only one MLLM response per query, compared with 35 for DecAF, and achieves over 4×4\times faster inference. Measurement is conducted on an NVIDIA H800 GPU.

Motion-grounded Video Reasoning Performance.

GroundMoRe (Deng et al., 2025) is a challenging benchmark that requires joint spatio-temporal reasoning to understand object motions and interactions from causal, sequential, counterfactual, and descriptive perspectives. The results in Table 11 show that ReVEAL achieves an overall 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} result of 37.1%, outperforming MORA (27.2%) by 9.9%. Notably, ReVEAL delivers substantial gains on both Causal and Descriptive questions, improving the scores from 27.4% to 37.7% and from 29.6% to 44.8%, respectively. These gains suggest that our thinking-with-video paradigm facilitates causal reasoning, while attention-derived latent evidence provides a video-wide perspective for tracking moving targets more accurately.

C.2 Additional Ablation Studies

Sensitivity to the CAGL Weights.

Table 13 evaluates the sensitivity of CAGL to its loss weights. Overall, ReVEAL maintains relatively stable performance across different weight configurations, indicating robustness to these hyperparameters. We adopt λCAGL=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{CAGL}}=0.2 and λrep=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}=0.1, which achieves the best performance on both benchmarks.

VET Fusion Strategies on Qwen2.5VL-7B.

Table 13 extends the VET fusion ablation to Qwen2.5VL-7B. Unlike Qwen3VL-8B, this backbone benefits most from background suppression, which improves attention-derived and SAM2 mask 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} by 4.6% and 1.9% on ReasonVOS, respectively. Fusing all three VET types achieves the best overall performance on both benchmarks, supporting the effectiveness of our role design and fusion strategy across MLLM backbones.

DALR Top-kk Ablation.

We evaluate DALR with different top-kk settings, each used during both training and inference. As shown in Table 15, selecting k=6k=6 layers achieves the best overall performance across the two benchmarks. Selecting more layers provides no consistent gains and may introduce additional noise into the grounding evidence.

DALR Selection Distribution.

Figure 7 shows DALR’s layer selection distribution on Ref-DAVIS with k=6k=6. The selected layer combinations vary across inputs, indicating input-dependent selection rather than reliance on a fixed subset.

Sensitivity to the Background Suppression Weight.

Figure 8 analyzes the effect of the background suppression weight α<BG>\alpha_{\texttt{<BG>}} on attention-derived and SAM2 mask quality. Since <BG> attention often covers broad non- foreground regions, it helps suppress diffuse or spurious object attention. The required suppression strength varies across backbones due to differences in their object attention patterns. ReVEAL-Qwen3VL-8B and ReVEAL-Qwen2.5VL-7B achieve the best SAM2 performance at α<BG>=0.1\alpha_{\texttt{<BG>}}=0.1 and 0.50.5, respectively. While stronger suppression generally improves attention-derived masks, overly large weights can also remove useful target evidence and degrade final segmentation.

Number of Sampled Point Prompts.

Table 15 studies the maximum number of points sampled from the fused attention map as visual prompts for SAM2 at inference time. Across all three benchmarks, increasing the number of sampled points yields no consistent performance gains. The default setting provides the best overall trade-off between mask quality and prompt efficiency.

Appendix D More Visualizations

This section provides additional qualitative results of ReVEAL, including comparisons with other methods, more role-specific visualizations, and failure cases.

D.1 More Comparisons with Other Methods

Figure 9 compares a representative case from ReasonVOS between ReVEAL and the Without-CoT paradigm. In this example, ReVEAL improves attention-mask 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} by only 1.7% over Without-CoT, yet its VET attention consistently favors the true target despite some hallucinated responses, whereas Without-CoT favors a visually similar distractor. Attention-mask evaluation reflects the spatiotemporal coverage of regions retained after thresholding, whereas SAM2 uses point prompts sampled from high-confidence attention locations. A higher attention-mask score does not necessarily indicate more confident attention peaks on the target. Stronger attention peaks on the true target may therefore yield more reliable point prompts, helping explain the larger gain in SAM2 segmentation despite the modest improvement in attention-mask quality.

Figure 10 presents additional qualitative comparisons of the fused attention maps produced by ReVEAL and DecAF (Han et al., 2025). In dynamic scenes requiring target tracking across frames, ReVEAL maintains consistent and clear attention on the target, whereas DecAF tends to produce spurious activations and lose focus on the target in some cases.

D.2 More Role-Token Attention Map Visualizations

Figure 11, Figure 12, and Figure 13 provide additional CoT responses and attention maps for the role-specific VETs, following Fig.  5. ReVEAL dynamically uses suppressive VETs (<BG> and <NEG>) according to the reasoning content, with their presence and number varying across examples. The CoT reasoning itself establishes semantic associations between visual entities and their corresponding VETs, enabling individual VETs to attend to relevant regions to some extent. This lightweight association can reduce the reliance on precise region-level supervision for every <NEG> occurrence, which would otherwise incur additional annotation cost. As shown in Figure 12 and 13, different <NEG> occurrences tend to highlight distinct distractor regions.

D.3 Failure Case Analysis and Limitations

Failure cases.

Figure 14, 15, and 16 show representative failures caused by limited target visibility and instance-level ambiguity. When the target is fully occluded, has not yet appeared, or is visible only briefly, limited visual and temporal context may lead to spurious attention activations in irrelevant regions. When multiple visually similar objects are present, the MLLM may struggle to identify the referred target during CoT reasoning, causing VET attention to focus on incorrect instances.

Limitations.

Despite its effectiveness, ReVEAL has several limitations. First, the current <NEG> design may not adequately distinguish individual distractors when multiple visually similar objects appear in more complex scenes. Second, VET grounding can become unreliable when MLLM attention is diffuse or focused on irrelevant regions, particularly under severe occlusion. Third, the current uniform sampling strategy may miss frames containing key visual entities, leaving them absent from the model input. The resulting lack of visual context may limit the model’s ability to reason effectively and produce reliable latent visual evidence. Future work could explore lightweight optimizations centered on the MLLM’s own video reasoning for ReVOS. For example, a frame selection module inspired by GLUS (Lin et al., 2025) and CoT-RVS (Kao et al., 2025) could help retain informative frames. More broadly, we will explore extending this efficient MLLM-centric design to omni scenarios.
